chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
I asked him about old wine that is made into vinegar; he said: There is no harm (in it).
2. Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from Ibn Bukayr, from Ubayd ibn Zurara who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
about a man who takes wine and makes it into vinegar; he said: There is no harm.
3. From him, from Safwan, from Ibn Bukayr, from Ubayd ibn Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

that he said regarding a man who sold fresh grape juice, and the ruler detained it until it became wine, and its owner made it into vinegar; he said: When it changes from the name of wine, there is no harm with it.

key_terms.الْخَمْر: Wine (specifically the fermented grape drink, forbidden in its original state)
key_terms.الْعَتِيقَة: Old/Aged (referring to wine that has been kept for a period)
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: There is no harm (a legal phrase indicating permissibility or lack of objection)

ai.seo_question: Is wine that turns into vinegar still considered impure or forbidden in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: These narrations from al-Istibsar, featuring prominent companions like Zurara and Ubayd ibn Zurara, establish the principle of *taharat al-khamr* (purity of wine) and its transformation into *khal* (vinegar). The scholars emphasize that the change of state (*istihlak*) removes the impurity and prohibition, allowing consumption even if the conversion was not natural, provided the identity of 'wine' is lost. This ruling is foundational in Shia fiqh for determining the purity of fermented products used in food or medicine.
